title: Count the Number of Incremovable Subarrays I
statement:
You get an array `nums` of positive integers. Call a non-empty contiguous block of `nums` *incremovable* when cutting it out leaves the remaining elements, in their original order, strictly increasing (each value larger than the one before it). If nothing remains, that counts as strictly increasing.

Return how many incremovable blocks `nums` has. Blocks are counted by position, so two blocks with the same values at different places count separately.
notes:
## Intuition

With at most 50 numbers there are at most 1,275 blocks to cut out, so we can afford to try every one. For each choice we just walk over the elements that stay and check that every value beats the one kept before it.

## Approach

1. Count in `count`, starting at 0.
2. Choose every block `start..end` with `start <= end` (the block may not be empty).
3. Walk every index `k`, skipping those inside the block. Keep the last kept value in `previous` (starting at `-Infinity`, so the first kept value always passes).
4. If a kept value is not larger than `previous`, mark `increasing` false and stop the walk.
5. If the walk finished with `increasing` still true, add one to `count`.
6. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]`. With `start = 0, end = 0` the kept values are `2, 3, 4`: each beats `previous`, so `count = 1`. Every other block behaves the same way, because what is left of an increasing array is still increasing, even when nothing is left (`start = 0, end = 3`). All `4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10` blocks pass, so the answer is `10`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³): O(n²) blocks, each checked with one O(n) walk.
- Space: O(1): only a few counters.

## Pitfalls

- The order must be *strictly* increasing: `[6, 6]` does not pass, so compare with `<=`.
- Removing the whole array is allowed and always counts, because an empty remainder is increasing.
- The check must also compare the values on both sides of the gap (`nums[start - 1]` with `nums[end + 1]`); walking the kept elements in order does that for free.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `count` | incremovable blocks found so far |
| `start`, `end` | first and last index of the block being removed |
| `k` | index walked while checking what remains |
| `previous` | last kept value seen in the walk |
| `increasing` | whether the kept values are still strictly increasing |

narration.5: Pick where the removed block begins.
narration.6: Pick where it ends; end starts at start, so the block is never empty.
narration.7: Before the walk nothing is kept, so any first value will be larger.
narration.9: Walk every index of the array to check what remains.
narration.10: Indices inside the removed block are skipped.
narration.13: A kept value that does not beat the previous one breaks the strict order.
narration.15: No need to look further for this block.
narration.17: This value becomes the one the next kept value must beat.
narration.19: The walk found no violation, so this block is incremovable.
narration.24: Every block has been tried; return the total.
